reviews.one_line_contribution: An item-level partition of agent failures into coverage failures (gold never sampled) and selection failures (gold sampled but outvoted), used to (a) derive a measured 'recoverable-coverage ceiling' bounding what any memory bank can buy, (b) adjudicate agreement-gated memory against agreement-gated extra sampling at matched tokens, and (c) test whether an instruction optimizer and a self-editing memory repair near-disjoint item sets.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Two works the proposal never cites threaten it more than the ones it concedes. (1) Brown et al., 'Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling' (2024), and the verifier/reranking line it sits in (Cobbe et al. 2021; Li et al. 2023), already decompose repeated-sampling performance into exactly coverage (is the answer in the sample set) versus selection/verification (can you pick it), and already show coverage rising with n while selection lags. The proposal's E0 stratification is that decomposition with SOLVED split by vote share; presenting it as 'what survives as ours' is not sustainable once a reviewer names this line. (2) Mallen et al., 'When Not to Trust Language Models' (ACL 2023) established that retrieval augmentation *hurts* precisely the questions the model already answers confidently and gated retrieval on that basis; the proposal's signature mechanistic claim — 'injection's damage falls almost entirely on high-agreement already-solved items' — is the same finding with vote-share substituted for entity popularity, and the Self-RAG/FLARE/Adaptive-RAG citations given do not cover it. What remains genuinely unclaimed after these two, plus the conceded MemRL/MemDelta/Evo-Memory protocol collisions and the Adaptive-Consistency gate collision, is narrow: the AGM-vs-AGS control and the stratum-decomposed disjointness test in E7.
reviews.strongest_objection: The coverage/selection partition is not a property of the model or the item; it is a property of the base prompt, temperature and n used to label it, and both load-bearing claims are damaged by this. (i) The Short Hypothesis and Abstract assert that 'sampling and instruction edits can only convert selection failures' and that 'injected experience is the only mechanism that can convert coverage failures.' The first half is simply false: raising n raises coverage — that is what pass@k growth *is* — and the paper's own decisive competitor AGS spends its gated budget on additional memory-free samples, i.e. on the one intervention that most directly attacks COVERAGE-FAIL@8. So the mechanistic story predicts AGM > AGS for a reason the experiment disproves by construction, and pool A's own 24 rollouts will show COVERAGE-FAIL@8 items whose gold appears by n=16 or 24. The 'recoverable-coverage ceiling' is therefore a function of the sampling configuration used to define it, not a ceiling on memory, and P8's claim that the coverage stratum shrinks at 14B is confounded with the fact that a stronger model's stratum was labelled at the same fixed n=8 and T=0.7. (ii) In a *tool-using* ReAct agent, instruction edits change search queries, hop order and stopping behaviour, hence change which documents enter context and which answers are reachable at all. GEPA-optimized instructions can and routinely do manufacture answers that never appeared under the base prompt — that is a coverage fix, not a selection fix. P6 predicts INSTR's fixes are ≤15% COVERAGE-FAIL; for a retrieval agent the more likely outcome is the opposite, and because strata are labelled by the *base* memory-free agent, any INSTR fix on an item whose trajectory changed is scored against a reference frame that no longer describes that condition. Either way the 'division of labour' theory is not identified by E7: a pass is partly definitional (strata frozen at the base prompt), and a failure is over-determined by the agentic setting rather than informative about instructions vs. memory. Secondary, but it will be raised: the study pre-commits to a bounded null in the one regime the proposal itself argues is most favourable to sampling (short factoid answers where majority vote is well defined), while explicitly scoping out the long-horizon procedural tasks where ExpeL/Reflexion/ReasoningBank actually claim their wins — so a null here does not qualify the literature it is aimed at.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Four concrete changes, roughly in order of importance. (1) Stop treating strata as fixed labels and report the coverage-conversion matrix: label each item's stratum at every budget point n ∈ {8,16,24} from pool A, publish coverage@n saturation curves, and state the recoverable-coverage ceiling as a function of n rather than a scalar. If the ceiling collapses when n rises to the AGS budget, that is the paper's real result and it should be the headline, not a footnote. It costs nothing — pool A already contains the rollouts. (2) Re-label strata per condition as well as by the base agent for E7, and report both frames; specifically report, for INSTR, how many fixes are items whose *retrieval trajectory* changed, since those are coverage fixes attributable to instructions and they directly test the theory's central asymmetry. (3) Add the two omitted arms named below. (4) Actually run the committed literature search before claiming novelty, and drop or heavily requalify P2's mechanism as a replication of Mallen-style 'retrieval harms what the model already knows' at the vote-share level rather than a new finding. Optionally, add one procedural/agentic task with a verifier-based best-of-n aggregation so the null, if it comes, is not confined to the regime where nobody claimed memory wins.
reviews.missing_baseline: Two. (a) **Agreement-gated extra retrieval (AGR)** — on the same low-agreement items and at matched tokens, spend the gated budget on more search calls, query reformulation, or a larger retrieval top-k instead of on injected experience. In multi-hop QA over a local index, a coverage failure is usually a failed bridge-entity retrieval, so this is the obvious and much cheaper way to convert coverage failures. Without it, even a clean AGM > AGS win cannot support 'injected experience is the only mechanism that converts coverage failures' — the paper would have shown only that memory beats *more samples*, not that it beats *more retrieval*. Its absence is the single clearest hole in E3, whose baseline list runs to six arms and omits the one that attacks the same stratum. (b) **An optimizer-selected demonstration baseline** (MIPRO / DSPy bootstrapped few-shot with random search over demonstration slots, fixed at test time, no self-editing). The track's framing is 'optimizer owns instructions, memory owns demonstrations'; E7 deliberately fits the instruction slot only, which means the demonstration slot is only ever occupied by retrieved memory. Pool D (retrieved solved exemplars) is not a substitute — it is retrieval-based, not optimizer-selected. Without a static optimized-demonstration arm, P6's disjointness result cannot distinguish 'memory is doing something instructions cannot' from 'demonstrations are doing something instructions cannot, and any demonstration source would do'.
reviews.preprint_collision: The check is, by its own admission, empty: the search tool hit a session-wide usage limit and returned no results, so this round contributes zero new evidence and the positioning is explicitly carried over and 'unverified as of now'. The proposal deserves credit for refusing to launder the failure into a novelty claim, and for having already demoted two claims (compute-matching, free gate) after earlier searches — that is more honest than most submissions. But honesty about an unsearched claim does not make it searched: as submitted, novelty is asserted, not established, and the commitment to search 'before submission' is exactly the work a reviewer is being asked to take on faith. Concretely, the carried-over list is also incomplete in ways a working search would likely have caught: it names no coverage-vs-selection decomposition from the repeated-sampling literature (Large Language Monkeys and successors), and no popularity/confidence-gated retrieval work showing retrieval harms already-known items (Mallen et al. 2023; SKR; the self-knowledge-gated RAG line), which is the nearest prior statement of the proposal's own P2 mechanism. The proposed query list also omits the terms most likely to surface a collision — 'coverage vs precision repeated sampling', 'when does retrieval hurt', 'confidence-gated retrieval', 'pass@k maj@k gap' — and searches only for memory-framed phrasings of a claim whose closest relatives are phrased in sampling and RAG terms. I score this as a weakness, not a neutral: the two surviving contributions (AGM-vs-AGS, stratum-level disjointness) are plausibly novel to me, but that is my prior, not the proposal's evidence.

reviews.one_line_contribution: The claim is that an item-level partition of memory-free failures into coverage failures (gold never sampled in n draws) versus selection failures (gold sampled but outvoted) predicts a mechanism-level division of labour — injected experience can only convert coverage failures, instruction optimization only selection failures, and injection damage lands on high-agreement solved items — plus the control that follows from it (agreement-gated memory vs. agreement-gated extra plain sampling at matched tokens, E3-i/P4) and the stratum-decomposed disjointness test between GEPA-style instruction search and a self-editing bank (E7/P6).
reviews.closest_prior_work: The proposal concedes MemRL, MemDelta, Evo-Memory, 2511.04234 and the Adaptive-Consistency line, but it never names the work that actually threatens the surviving contribution: the coverage-vs-selection partition IS the pass@k-minus-maj@k decomposition, introduced and named as coverage versus verification/selection in Brown et al., 'Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling' (2024), and used throughout the repeated-sampling and verifier-selection literature (Chen et al. 'Are More LLM Calls All You Need?'; the pass@k-vs-pass@1 RLVR debate; verifier-free best-of-n work). The 'recoverable-coverage ceiling' is oracle-gated pass@k analysis with a new name. What is genuinely unclaimed by that line is only the *attribution* use — bucketing an intervention's fixes and breaks by the sampler's coverage/selection stratum — which is a modest analytic move, not a new object. E3-i (AGS) is likewise the natural application of Adaptive-Consistency's own control to a memory arm; MemRL already puts Pass@k sampling beside memory under one protocol, which is most of P1. Novelty therefore rests on the E7 disjointness test, and that test as specified is not decisive (see strongest_objection).
reviews.strongest_objection: P6, the only prediction carrying the track's headline coupling question, cannot fail in its stated form. Jaccard overlap < 0.25 between INSTR's and MEM's fixed-item sets is what two *independent* interventions produce by chance: the pilot reports GEPA fixing roughly as many items as it breaks (order tens of items) and the motivating anomaly reports the bank fixing zero and breaking six to seven, so the two fix sets will be small sets drawn from ~200-300 wrong items, and their expected chance Jaccard is well under 0.10. The proposal states no permutation/chance-overlap null conditioned on each mechanism's marginal fix count and per-item difficulty, so 'disjoint' will be declared whether or not the mechanisms are actually complementary. The same defect sinks P2's first clause: '≥60% of memory's fixes fall in COVERAGE-FAIL' is a share, not a rate, and is uninformative without the stratum base rates — if COVERAGE-FAIL is 15% of items and SELECTION-FAIL is 10%, a proportional, mechanism-free scatter of fixes already clears 60%. The prediction that tests the mechanism is fix *rate per stratum* (fixes / stratum size), and it is not the one pre-registered. Compounding this, all of E7 and P2's fix-side analysis has an empty-denominator risk the power section never addresses: the 800-item, 3.1-point MDE is computed for a global accuracy contrast, while P6 and P2 are statements about the composition of maybe 10-30 fixed items per arm. If the pilot's 'fixed zero items' replicates, memory's fix set is empty and P2/P6/P4's 'advantage concentrated in COVERAGE-FAIL' are undefined rather than refuted, and the paper is left with the bounded null plus E0's ceiling — i.e. one more compute-matched replication of MemRL/MemDelta on a smaller model.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: (1) Re-pre-register P6 as an overlap odds ratio against a permutation null that fixes each mechanism's marginal fix count and strata/difficulty, with a stated MDE for that statistic, and re-pre-register P2 as per-stratum fix and break *rates* with confidence intervals rather than shares of a total. (2) State the minimum fix count under which E7 and P2 are declared uninformative-by-design, and add a pre-committed fallback (e.g. pooling INSTR fixes across strata, or raising the optimizer budget) so the arm cannot silently return an undefined answer. (3) Show that the stratum labels are stable, not an artifact of n=8: pool A's 24 rollouts permit a re-label at n=16 or n=24; report the COVERAGE-FAIL churn rate between disjoint 8-draws and the fraction of n=8 COVERAGE-FAIL items covered at n=24, since any item with small nonzero gold mass is relabelled by resampling alone and will be 'fixed' by any perturbation, memory or not. (4) Add the extra-retrieval control named below, without which P4 does not license the sentence in the title. (5) Say explicitly whether E6's online reflector sees gold answers or correctness feedback when writing entries from held-out rollouts; if it does, the online arm is transductive label leakage across the 800 evaluation items and its ceiling gain in P7 is not comparable to the static bank, and if it does not, the write path differs from the static bank's and confounds contrast (a). (6) Decompose P7, which is currently a four-way conjunction with no stated reading for partial outcomes.
reviews.missing_baseline: Agreement-gated *extra retrieval* — spending the gated token budget on more search calls, more retrieved passages, or an extra hop rather than on injected experience or on extra samples. In multi-hop QA over a local Wikipedia index, a coverage failure is overwhelmingly a case where the supporting passage never entered the context, so the direct competitor to 'inject distilled experience on low-agreement items' is 'retrieve more documents on low-agreement items' at the same cost. The plan's AGS controls only for extra sampling, so a P4 win would leave the reviewer's obvious alternative explanation — memory is a slow proxy for retrieval depth — untested, and Adaptive-RAG (dropped as 'redundant with the confidence gate') was exactly that control. Secondary omission: a content-matched but irrelevant injection arm at held-out (k tokens of random or off-task bank entries), which is the only way to separate the pilot's own finding that *volume*, not content, was the causal lever from the claim that experience content does the work; the k-sweep varies volume while holding content relevant and cannot make that separation.
reviews.preprint_collision: The check reports that the search tool hit a hard usage limit and returned nothing this round, and the authors correctly refuse to read that silence as novelty — the honesty is creditable but it does not substitute for the search. As submitted, the novelty claim is explicitly self-labelled 'unverified as of now' and rests on a carried-over search of unstated date, so by the standard that an unsearched novelty claim is a weakness, this is a weakness and not a neutral. Beyond the missing round, the carried-over check has a substantive blind spot: none of its queries ('compute-matched agent memory', 'self-consistency vs experience retrieval', 'when does retrieved experience hurt', 'coverage vs selection failure sampling', 'prompt optimization and memory division of labour') would surface the repeated-sampling literature where the coverage/selection split originates (Large Language Monkeys and its successors), and no such work is cited anywhere in the proposal — so the one contribution the authors say survives has not been searched for under its established name. The committed pre-submission search must add queries for pass@k vs maj@k, coverage vs verification gap, and sample-selection bottleneck, and must check for 2026 preprints attributing agent-memory gains to sample-selection versus generation, which is the live area most likely to hold a direct collision.

reviews.one_line_contribution: Partition an agent's memory-free failures at a fixed sample budget into coverage failures (gold never generated) and selection failures (gold generated but outvoted), argue that injected experience can only repair the former while instruction optimization repairs the latter, and adjudicate memory's residual value with an agreement-gated-memory vs. agreement-gated-extra-sampling control at matched tokens (P4) plus a stratum-decomposed disjointness test between GEPA-style instructions and a self-editing bank (P6).
reviews.closest_prior_work: The coverage/selection split is not new; it is the pass@k-vs-maj@k (coverage vs. precision) decomposition of Brown et al., 'Large Language Monkeys' (arXiv:2407.21787), and the argument that a mechanism which only reweights already-sampled candidates cannot manufacture new ones is the central claim of the RLVR pass@k line (e.g. Yue et al., arXiv:2504.13837, 'Does RLVR Incentivize Reasoning Capacity Beyond the Base Model?'), which reaches it for RL post-training exactly as this proposal reaches it for instruction edits. Neither is cited anywhere in Related Work or the collision check. What genuinely survives is narrower than the proposal states: transplanting that known decomposition onto the memory-vs-prompt-optimizer question and running the AGS control. On the memory side, Evo-Memory (2511.20857) and arXiv:2511.04234 already report the likely headline (a trivial or memory-free baseline beats elaborate experience reuse at matched compute), and Difficulty-Adaptive SC already conditions low-agreement items on retrieved solved exemplars — which the proposal concedes and now runs as E3-ii, i.e. its nearest neighbour is inside its own baseline table.
reviews.strongest_objection: COVERAGE-FAIL is operationalized as 'gold absent from 8 samples of pool A', which makes it a property of the budget, not of the item — and the AGS arm in E3/P4 spends its extra tokens on precisely the low-agreement items whose gold answer has small but nonzero sampling probability. So the theory's load-bearing asymmetry ('sampling can only convert selection failures; only injected experience converts coverage failures') is false as implemented, and P4's mechanism attribution ('AGM's advantage concentrated in COVERAGE-FAIL') is confounded with the fact that AGS attacks the same stratum. This compounds with a power problem the Measurement section never addresses: the MDE analysis powers accuracy contrasts (3.1 points ≈ 25 net discordant items), but every mechanism prediction is a composition statistic over memory's fix set — and the proposal's own pilot says the bank fixed ZERO items and P1/P7 predict always-on memory loses. If MEM yields ~10 fixes, P2's '≥60% of fixes in COVERAGE-FAIL' has a confidence interval spanning most of the unit interval, and P6's 'Jaccard overlap < 0.25' is satisfied degenerately by an empty fix set rather than by any division of labour. P6 also asserts additivity 'within 1.5 points', a precision finer than the study's own 3.1-point MDE, so it cannot be established at n=800 in either direction. The paper's two declared legs (P2 mechanism, P6 coupling) are therefore unpowered as specified, leaving a bounded null on one Wikipedia multi-hop task with one 7B model — a result Evo-Memory and 2511.04234 substantially already report.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: (1) Report the coverage curve from pool A — fraction of items where gold first appears at n = 1,2,4,8,16,24 — and redefine COVERAGE-FAIL asymptotically (absent from all 24) with an explicit measured conversion rate of extra sampling inside that stratum; the recoverable-coverage ceiling then has to be stated net of what AGS itself recovers, otherwise E0's go/no-go number is inflated. (2) Add a power analysis for the stratum-composition statistics, and pre-register a minimum fix-count precondition (e.g. ≥40 MEM fixes and ≥40 INSTR fixes) below which P2/P6/P7 are reported as descriptive rather than as confirmatory tests; note explicitly that Jaccard is undefined when a fix set is near-empty and pre-specify the fallback. (3) Restate P6 as an equivalence test with a bound at or above the MDE, or reallocate items from the free pool reads to enlarge the E7 held-out set. (4) Run the coverage-targeted memory-free control described below, so P4 is against the strongest cheap coverage mechanism rather than against more T=0.7 samples. (5) Stop describing HotpotQA-distractor + HoVer as breadth — both are Wikipedia multi-hop EM tasks — and either add a genuinely different family or scope every claim to answer-aggregation Wikipedia QA in the title. (6) Cite and position against the pass@k coverage/precision line; it is the proposal's actual intellectual antecedent.
reviews.missing_baseline: Two. First and decisive: a coverage-targeted memory-free gated arm — same τ and n0, matched tokens, but the extra samples drawn at higher temperature and/or under prompt perturbation / diverse decoding (the proposal cuts the temperature sweep, and it cites arXiv:2608.09351 showing input-side diversity Pareto-dominates plain SC at matched cost). AGS as specified redraws at the identical T=0.7 from the identical prompt, which is the weakest possible coverage mechanism; if AGM beats that AGS but loses to a high-temperature or perturbed AGS, P4 collapses and the paper's decisive contrast was rigged toward memory. Second: memory-as-reranker — retrieved experience used only to select among pool-A candidates at answer time, never placed in the generation prefix. It is nearly free from existing pools, has zero SOLVED-HIGH breakage by construction, and is the obvious engineering response to the paper's own mechanism (memory helps coverage, hurts selection); a reviewer will ask why the proposal tests only prefix injection and then generalizes to 'agent memory'.
reviews.preprint_collision: Weak, and the proposal says so itself: this round's search returned nothing because the tool hit a hard usage limit, so the positioning is explicitly carried over and unverified. Per the standard that an unsearched novelty claim is a weakness rather than a neutral, this costs the submission — the commitment to 'run a structured search before submission' is not evidence available at review time. Beyond the tool failure, the check is thin in the exact place novelty is claimed: its query list ('coverage vs selection failure sampling') never surfaces the pass@k coverage/precision literature (Large Language Monkeys 2407.21787; the RLVR-pass@k line, e.g. 2504.13837; verification-bottleneck work on sample-scrutinize-scale), which is where the surviving conceptual contribution actually originates. I cannot name a preprint that runs the exact AGM-vs-AGS control with a stratum decomposition over agent memory, so the specific control looks unclaimed; but the two conceded collisions (MemRL 2601.03192, MemDelta 2606.29914) plus Evo-Memory 2511.20857 and 2511.04234 already occupy the compute-matched-memory-loses conclusion, which is the outcome the proposal's own pilot and P1/P7 predict it will reach.
